title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 4.2.1 Reading: Intensive Reading (Visuals)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Visuals are pictures, cartoons, comics, photographs, signs and maps that carry information. In this sub-strand you will read them in books and on a screen, say what they mean, and use a simple map to give directions with the words north, south, east and west. The pictures are about road safety and first aid.

## Strand 4.0: Accidents - First Aid
Sub-strand 4.2.1: Reading: Intensive Reading (Visuals)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) read visuals in print and digital formats for information
b) interpret visual media appropriately for comprehension
c) acknowledge the importance of visual media for lifelong learning

## What this sub-strand covers
• Interpreting visuals

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is it important to interpret visuals correctly?
2. How do visuals like photos and videos enhance our understanding of a text?

## Core competencies
• Digital Literacy: This is enhanced as the learner uses technology to conduct virtual tours on google maps and find the direction of various places on the map.
• Learning to Learn: The is developed as the learner builds on their learning experience by locating information from a simple map and make short sentences.

## Values
• Unity: It is developed as the learner works together with peers as they discuss and interpret visuals.
• Love: This is enhanced as the learner appreciates views from peers when viewing and interpreting visuals.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem: This is developed as the learner is able to interpret visuals independently for information and directions in their daily experiences.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner relates the concept of interpreting visuals with their learning of concepts such as map reading in Social Studies.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 4.0 Accidents- First Aid, Sub-strand 4.2.1 Intensive Reading: Visuals

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Reading pictures, cartoons and comics

LESSON 1: READING PICTURES, CARTOONS AND COMICS
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Name what is happening in a picture, cartoon or comic.
• Predict what may happen next and give a reason from the visual.
• Explain how a video or animation can add information that a still picture cannot.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read visuals in print and digital formats for information; b) interpret visual media appropriately for comprehension

## Introduction
A sign, a comic or a short video can warn you faster than a long paragraph. The skill is to look carefully, name what you see, and check that your meaning matches the picture.

## Notes
### What a visual is
A visual is information you take in with your eyes. It may be a photograph, a drawing, a cartoon, a comic, a mime or a video. A mime is a story told with actions and no words. Print visuals are on paper. Digital visuals are on a screen, such as an animation or a video clip.

### How to read a still picture
Look in this order:

- Who or what is in the picture?
- Where is the scene, and what objects can you name?
- What is happening right now?
- What do colours, arrows or labels add?
- What might happen next, and which detail makes you think so?

Do not guess a fact the picture does not show. If nobody is bleeding, do not say there is a deep cut.

### A four-frame comic: The Wet Road
Frame 1. School is over. Dark clouds fill the sky. A sign shows people walking on a footbridge, not on the road.
Frame 2. Juma steps towards the road. Amina points to the footbridge and shakes her head.
Frame 3. A motorcycle comes round the bend. The two children are already on the footbridge.
Frame 4. They reach the gate. Amina points back at the wet road.

The comic does not show a crash. It shows a safe choice. A wet road can make a vehicle take longer to stop, so crossing in front of it is dangerous. A good prediction after Frame 2 is: they will use the footbridge. The sign and Amina's pointing support that prediction.

### Still picture or moving visual
A photograph freezes one moment. A video or animation can show the order of events, such as a barrier coming down at a railway crossing before a train passes. Sound can add a bell or a voice. You still ask the same questions: who, where, what is happening, and what it is telling me to do.

When you watch a digital story, sit where you can see, listen once for the whole story, then watch again for details.

## Key words
• visual — information shown in a picture, sign, comic, map or video
• comic — a story told in a row of pictures, often with words in boxes or speech balloons
• predict — to say what you think will happen next, using clues you already have
• mime — a performance that tells a story with actions and no spoken words

## Worked examples

### Example 1
In Frame 2 of The Wet Road, what is Amina telling Juma?

Working:
1. Look at her action: she points to the footbridge and shakes her head.
2. Shaking the head means no. The sign in Frame 1 shows the safe path.

Answer: She is telling him not to cross the road and to use the footbridge.

### Example 2
Why is Frame 3 important?

Working:
1. A motorcycle appears on the road.
2. The children are already on the footbridge, so they are out of its way.

Answer: It shows that the footbridge kept them away from the motorcycle.

## Activity: Predict the next frame
You will need: The four-frame comic drawn on manila paper, or four picture cards, Pencils and paper
1. In groups, look at Frames 1 and 2 only. Each learner writes one sentence predicting what will happen next.
2. Reveal Frames 3 and 4. Compare your prediction with the comic and say which detail guided you.
3. One learner mimes a new road-safety moment, such as waiting at a railway crossing, while the group says what the mime means.
4. If your teacher plays a short age-appropriate video or animation, watch it twice and write two facts you saw.

## Practice
1. What is the difference between a photograph and a video?
2. Which clue in The Wet Road tells the children the safe place to cross?
3. Write one prediction you could make after Frame 1, and name the clue.

## Summary
• Read a visual by asking who, where, what is happening, and what may happen next.
• Use only the clues the picture gives.
• A video can show order and sound that a still picture cannot.

### Answers to practice
1. A photograph shows one frozen moment. A video shows events moving in order and may include sound.
2. The sign that shows people walking on the footbridge, and Amina pointing to it.
3. They will need shelter or a safe crossing because dark clouds show rain is coming, and the sign shows a footbridge.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Road safety pictures and a first aid poster

LESSON 2: ROAD SAFETY PICTURES AND A FIRST AID POSTER
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• Interpret pictures of an underpass, a footbridge, a luggage rack, a roundabout and a railway crossing.
• Read a simple first aid poster and say which help matches which injury.
• Explain why reading a visual wrongly can be unsafe.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read visuals in print and digital formats for information; b) interpret visual media appropriately for comprehension; c) acknowledge the importance of visual media for lifelong learning

## Introduction
Road signs and posters do their work only if we understand them. A picture of a train is not a decoration. It tells you to stop, look and listen before you cross.

## Notes
### Five places you may see in a picture
- A footbridge is a bridge for people on foot. It carries them over a road or railway.
- An underpass is a path that goes under a road or railway. People cross without stepping into traffic.
- A roundabout is a circular junction. Vehicles travel around a central island. People on foot should use a crossing, a footbridge or an underpass, not walk across the island between moving vehicles.
- A railway crossing is where a road crosses railway tracks. Stop, look both ways and listen. If a barrier is down, lights are flashing or a bell is ringing, wait until it is safe and the way is clear.
- A luggage rack is a shelf in a bus or train. Bags should sit fully on the rack so they do not slide off when the vehicle stops suddenly. Do not pile heavy boxes where they can fall on passengers, and do not leave bags in the aisle.

### Reading a first aid poster
Imagine a poster at a health centre with three pictures.

Picture A shows an adult washing hands, then rinsing a small cut with clean water, pressing a clean cloth on it, and covering it with a plaster.
Picture B shows a nosebleed. The person is sitting and leaning forward while an adult pinches the soft part of the nose.
Picture C shows a snake and an arrow pointing to a hospital.

Read each picture for its own message. Picture A is for a small cut only. If the bleeding will not stop, or the cut is deep, an adult should get medical help. Picture B means sit and lean forward, not backward, so blood does not run down the throat. Pinch the soft part of the nose and hold it for about ten minutes. If the bleeding continues after that, an adult should get medical help. Picture C means a snake bite is an emergency: keep the person calm and still, remove rings or tight items if that is easy, and let an adult take them to hospital at once. Do not cut the bite, suck it, or tie a tight band around the limb.

### Why the correct reading matters
If you mix up the pictures, you might treat a snake bite like a small cut. That delay can be harmful. Visuals help us learn for life because we meet signs, maps and posters long after we leave this class. We respect a classmate's idea, then we check it against what the picture actually shows.

## Key words
• footbridge — a bridge that people walk on to cross above a road or railway
• underpass — a path that goes under a road or railway so people can cross safely
• roundabout — a circular junction where vehicles travel around a central island
• railway crossing — the place where a road crosses railway tracks
• luggage rack — a shelf in a bus or train where passengers put their bags

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A picture shows a barrier down, red lights flashing and a train on the tracks. What should a pedestrian do?

Working:
1. Name the place: a railway crossing.
2. The barrier and lights mean the way is not clear.

Answer: Wait. Cross only when the barrier is up, the lights have stopped and the tracks are clear.

### Example 2
Which poster picture matches a snake bite: A, B or C?

Working:
1. Picture A is a small cut. Picture B is a nosebleed. Picture C shows a snake and a hospital.

Answer: Picture C. Keep the person still and get an adult to take them to hospital. Do not cut or suck the bite.

## Activity: Interpret the safety visuals
You will need: Pictures or drawings of a footbridge, an underpass, a roundabout, a railway crossing, a luggage rack and the three-part first aid poster, Exercise books
1. Work in a group. Place the pictures face up.
2. Each learner picks one picture, names it, and says what a person in the picture should do.
3. The group checks the meaning together and writes one sentence for each picture.
4. Discuss what could go wrong if someone read Picture C as if it were Picture A.

## Practice
1. What is the difference between a footbridge and an underpass?
2. How should a bag be placed on a luggage rack?
3. During a nosebleed, should the person tilt the head back? Why?

## Summary
• Footbridges and underpasses keep walkers away from vehicles.
• At a railway crossing, wait when barriers or warning lights say the way is not clear.
• Each picture on a first aid poster has its own instruction. A snake bite needs a hospital, not a plaster.

### Answers to practice
1. A footbridge goes over a road or railway. An underpass goes under it. Both let people cross away from vehicles.
2. It should sit fully on the rack so it cannot slide off when the vehicle stops. Heavy items should not be piled where they can fall, and bags should not block the aisle.
3. No. The person should sit and lean forward so that blood does not run down the throat. An adult pinches the soft part of the nose.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Maps, compass directions and digital maps

LESSON 3: MAPS, COMPASS DIRECTIONS AND DIGITAL MAPS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Find places on a simple map using north, south, east and west.
• Give a short direction from one place to another.
• Describe how a digital map can be used with an adult to find a direction.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read visuals in print and digital formats for information; b) interpret visual media appropriately for comprehension; c) acknowledge the importance of visual media for lifelong learning

## Introduction
If a visitor asks the way to the health centre, pointing vaguely is not enough. A map and the four directions let you give information another person can follow.

## Notes
### The four directions
North, south, east and west are the four main compass directions.

- On most printed maps, north is at the top, south at the bottom, east on the right and west on the left. Always check the compass rose, because a map can be turned.
- The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If you face the sunrise, north is on your left and south is on your right.

### A simple map of a school area
Look at a plan with the school in the middle.

- The health centre is north of the school.
- The market is east of the school.
- The railway crossing is south of the school.
- The footbridge is west of the school, over the main road.

Sentences from the map: The health centre is north of the school. The market is east of the school. From the school, walk south to reach the railway crossing, then stop, look and listen.

### Giving directions
Start at a place the listener knows. Name the direction and the landmark. 'From the school gate, walk west to the footbridge. Cross there, not on the road.' Keep the sentences short.

### Digital maps
A digital map, such as the maps you can open with a teacher on a tablet, lets you search for a place and see roads. Some phones show a dot for where you are standing. The map may rotate as you walk, so find the north marker before you decide which way to turn. Use it with an adult. Do not go off alone because a screen told you to.

A virtual tour means looking at a place on a digital map or street pictures without travelling there. You might find the school, then see whether the health centre lies to the north or the south. Write one sentence: 'The clinic is north of the school.' Maps are a lifelong tool for journeys, news and weather, so reading them carefully is worth the practice.

## Key words
• compass rose — the symbol on a map that shows where north, south, east and west are
• north — the direction towards the top of most maps; opposite of south
• landmark — a place or object you can recognise and use when giving directions
• digital map — a map on a screen that you can search and sometimes zoom

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Using the school map, which direction is the market from the school?

Working:
1. Find the school in the middle.
2. The market is on the east side.

Answer: East

### Example 2
Complete the sentence: The sun rises in the ____.

Working:
1. Recall the fact about sunrise.
2. Sunrise is in the east. Sunset is in the west.

Answer: east

### Example 3
Give a direction from the school to the footbridge.

Working:
1. The footbridge is west of the school.
2. Tell the listener to walk west and cross on the bridge.

Answer: From the school, walk west to the footbridge and cross the road there.

## Activity: Find it on the map
You will need: A printed simple map with a compass rose, A digital map opened by the teacher, if a device is available
1. In pairs, study the printed map. One learner asks, 'In which direction is the market from the school?' The partner answers in a full sentence.
2. Swap and give the direction to the health centre, the railway crossing and the footbridge.
3. With your teacher, open a digital map and search for a familiar place such as your school. Find the north marker before you describe a direction.
4. Write two sentences that use north, south, east or west.

## Practice
1. On most printed maps, which direction is at the top?
2. The railway crossing is south of the school. Write the direction you walk from the school to reach it.
3. Why should you check the compass rose on a digital map before you turn?
4. Write a sentence: The sun sets in the ____.

## Summary
• North, south, east and west tell us where places are.
• The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
• Use a digital map with an adult, and check which way is north.

### Answers to practice
1. North
2. Walk south.
3. The map may be rotated, so the top of the screen may not be north until you check the north marker.
4. The sun sets in the west.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 4.2.1 READING: INTENSIVE READING (VISUALS)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which question helps you read a picture?
   A. How many pages are in the book?
   B. Who is in the picture and what is happening?
   C. What is the writer's favourite colour?
   D. How heavy is the paper?

2. In The Wet Road, why do the children use the footbridge?
   A. To see the clouds more clearly
   B. To stay off the wet road when a motorcycle is coming
   C. To catch the motorcycle
   D. To play on the railway

3. A path that goes under a busy road is called
   A. a roundabout
   B. a luggage rack
   C. an underpass
   D. a number plate

4. At a railway crossing the barrier is down. What should you do?
   A. Duck under the barrier and run
   B. Wait until the way is clear
   C. Stand on the tracks to see the train
   D. Leave a bag on the tracks

5. A first aid poster shows a snake and an arrow to a hospital. The safe message is:
   A. Cover the bite with a plaster and keep playing
   B. Cut the bite and suck it
   C. Keep the person still and get an adult to take them to hospital
   D. Tie a tight band and wait at home

6. During a nosebleed the person should
   A. lie down and tilt the head back
   B. sit and lean forward
   C. run around to stay awake
   D. put soil on the nose

7. The sun rises in the
   A. north
   B. south
   C. east
   D. west

8. On the school map, the market is east of the school. The health centre is
   A. north of the school
   B. south of the school
   C. inside the roundabout
   D. on the railway tracks

9. Why do we learn to interpret visuals?
   A. So we can ignore signs
   B. So pictures, maps and posters give us the right information
   C. So we never need to read words
   D. So we can cross anywhere

10. Write one sentence giving a direction from the school to the footbridge on the map.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 4.2.1 READING: INTENSIVE READING (VISUALS)
========================================

1. B. Who is in the picture and what is happening?
   A visual is read by naming the people or objects and the action.

2. B. To stay off the wet road when a motorcycle is coming
   The comic shows them on the footbridge while a motorcycle uses the road.

3. C. an underpass
   An underpass lets people pass underneath the road.

4. B. Wait until the way is clear
   A lowered barrier means it is not safe to cross.

5. C. Keep the person still and get an adult to take them to hospital
   A snake bite is an emergency. Do not cut, suck or tightly tie the limb.

6. B. sit and lean forward
   Leaning forward helps keep blood from running down the throat.

7. C. east
   Sunrise is in the east. Sunset is in the west.

8. A. north of the school
   The map places the health centre to the north.

9. B. So pictures, maps and posters give us the right information
   A correct reading keeps the message clear and can keep us safe.

10. From the school, walk west to the footbridge.
   The footbridge is west of the school, so the direction sentence uses west.

## Practice
1. What is the difference between a photograph and a video?
2. Which clue in The Wet Road tells the children the safe place to cross?
3. Write one prediction you could make after Frame 1, and name the clue.

## Summary
• Read a visual by asking who, where, what is happening, and what may happen next.
• Use only the clues the picture gives.
• A video can show order and sound that a still picture cannot.

### Answers to practice
1. A photograph shows one frozen moment. A video shows events moving in order and may include sound.
2. The sign that shows people walking on the footbridge, and Amina pointing to it.
3. They will need shelter or a safe crossing because dark clouds show rain is coming, and the sign shows a footbridge.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Road safety pictures and a first aid poster
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: ROAD SAFETY PICTURES AND A FIRST AID POSTER
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• Interpret pictures of an underpass, a footbridge, a luggage rack, a roundabout and a railway crossing.
• Read a simple first aid poster and say which help matches which injury.
• Explain why reading a visual wrongly can be unsafe.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read visuals in print and digital formats for information; b) interpret visual media appropriately for comprehension; c) acknowledge the importance of visual media for lifelong learning

## Introduction
Road signs and posters do their work only if we understand them. A picture of a train is not a decoration. It tells you to stop, look and listen before you cross.

## Notes
### Five places you may see in a picture
- A footbridge is a bridge for people on foot. It carries them over a road or railway.
- An underpass is a path that goes under a road or railway. People cross without stepping into traffic.
- A roundabout is a circular junction. Vehicles travel around a central island. People on foot should use a crossing, a footbridge or an underpass, not walk across the island between moving vehicles.
- A railway crossing is where a road crosses railway tracks. Stop, look both ways and listen. If a barrier is down, lights are flashing or a bell is ringing, wait until it is safe and the way is clear.
- A luggage rack is a shelf in a bus or train. Bags should sit fully on the rack so they do not slide off when the vehicle stops suddenly. Do not pile heavy boxes where they can fall on passengers, and do not leave bags in the aisle.

### Reading a first aid poster
Imagine a poster at a health centre with three pictures.

Picture A shows an adult washing hands, then rinsing a small cut with clean water, pressing a clean cloth on it, and covering it with a plaster.
Picture B shows a nosebleed. The person is sitting and leaning forward while an adult pinches the soft part of the nose.
Picture C shows a snake and an arrow pointing to a hospital.

Read each picture for its own message. Picture A is for a small cut only. If the bleeding will not stop, or the cut is deep, an adult should get medical help. Picture B means sit and lean forward, not backward, so blood does not run down the throat. Pinch the soft part of the nose and hold it for about ten minutes. If the bleeding continues after that, an adult should get medical help. Picture C means a snake bite is an emergency: keep the person calm and still, remove rings or tight items if that is easy, and let an adult take them to hospital at once. Do not cut the bite, suck it, or tie a tight band around the limb.

### Why the correct reading matters
If you mix up the pictures, you might treat a snake bite like a small cut. That delay can be harmful. Visuals help us learn for life because we meet signs, maps and posters long after we leave this class. We respect a classmate's idea, then we check it against what the picture actually shows.

## Key words
• footbridge — a bridge that people walk on to cross above a road or railway
• underpass — a path that goes under a road or railway so people can cross safely
• roundabout — a circular junction where vehicles travel around a central island
• railway crossing — the place where a road crosses railway tracks
• luggage rack — a shelf in a bus or train where passengers put their bags

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A picture shows a barrier down, red lights flashing and a train on the tracks. What should a pedestrian do?

Working:
1. Name the place: a railway crossing.
2. The barrier and lights mean the way is not clear.

Answer: Wait. Cross only when the barrier is up, the lights have stopped and the tracks are clear.

### Example 2
Which poster picture matches a snake bite: A, B or C?

Working:
1. Picture A is a small cut. Picture B is a nosebleed. Picture C shows a snake and a hospital.

Answer: Picture C. Keep the person still and get an adult to take them to hospital. Do not cut or suck the bite.

## Activity: Interpret the safety visuals
You will need: Pictures or drawings of a footbridge, an underpass, a roundabout, a railway crossing, a luggage rack and the three-part first aid poster, Exercise books
1. Work in a group. Place the pictures face up.
2. Each learner picks one picture, names it, and says what a person in the picture should do.
3. The group checks the meaning together and writes one sentence for each picture.
4. Discuss what could go wrong if someone read Picture C as if it were Picture A.

## Practice
1. What is the difference between a footbridge and an underpass?
2. How should a bag be placed on a luggage rack?
3. During a nosebleed, should the person tilt the head back? Why?

## Summary
• Footbridges and underpasses keep walkers away from vehicles.
• At a railway crossing, wait when barriers or warning lights say the way is not clear.
• Each picture on a first aid poster has its own instruction. A snake bite needs a hospital, not a plaster.

### Answers to practice
1. A footbridge goes over a road or railway. An underpass goes under it. Both let people cross away from vehicles.
2. It should sit fully on the rack so it cannot slide off when the vehicle stops. Heavy items should not be piled where they can fall, and bags should not block the aisle.
3. No. The person should sit and lean forward so that blood does not run down the throat. An adult pinches the soft part of the nose.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Maps, compass directions and digital maps
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: MAPS, COMPASS DIRECTIONS AND DIGITAL MAPS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Find places on a simple map using north, south, east and west.
• Give a short direction from one place to another.
• Describe how a digital map can be used with an adult to find a direction.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read visuals in print and digital formats for information; b) interpret visual media appropriately for comprehension; c) acknowledge the importance of visual media for lifelong learning

## Introduction
If a visitor asks the way to the health centre, pointing vaguely is not enough. A map and the four directions let you give information another person can follow.

## Notes
### The four directions
North, south, east and west are the four main compass directions.

- On most printed maps, north is at the top, south at the bottom, east on the right and west on the left. Always check the compass rose, because a map can be turned.
- The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If you face the sunrise, north is on your left and south is on your right.

### A simple map of a school area
Look at a plan with the school in the middle.

- The health centre is north of the school.
- The market is east of the school.
- The railway crossing is south of the school.
- The footbridge is west of the school, over the main road.

Sentences from the map: The health centre is north of the school. The market is east of the school. From the school, walk south to reach the railway crossing, then stop, look and listen.

### Giving directions
Start at a place the listener knows. Name the direction and the landmark. 'From the school gate, walk west to the footbridge. Cross there, not on the road.' Keep the sentences short.

### Digital maps
A digital map, such as the maps you can open with a teacher on a tablet, lets you search for a place and see roads. Some phones show a dot for where you are standing. The map may rotate as you walk, so find the north marker before you decide which way to turn. Use it with an adult. Do not go off alone because a screen told you to.

A virtual tour means looking at a place on a digital map or street pictures without travelling there. You might find the school, then see whether the health centre lies to the north or the south. Write one sentence: 'The clinic is north of the school.' Maps are a lifelong tool for journeys, news and weather, so reading them carefully is worth the practice.

[DIAGRAM]

ALT: A simple map: health centre to the north, market to the east, footbridge to the west, railway crossing to the south

## Key words
• compass rose — the symbol on a map that shows where north, south, east and west are
• north — the direction towards the top of most maps; opposite of south
• landmark — a place or object you can recognise and use when giving directions
• digital map — a map on a screen that you can search and sometimes zoom

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Using the school map, which direction is the market from the school?

Working:
1. Find the school in the middle.
2. The market is on the east side.

Answer: East

### Example 2
Complete the sentence: The sun rises in the ____.

Working:
1. Recall the fact about sunrise.
2. Sunrise is in the east. Sunset is in the west.

Answer: east

### Example 3
Give a direction from the school to the footbridge.

Working:
1. The footbridge is west of the school.
2. Tell the listener to walk west and cross on the bridge.

Answer: From the school, walk west to the footbridge and cross the road there.

## Activity: Find it on the map
You will need: A printed simple map with a compass rose, A digital map opened by the teacher, if a device is available
1. In pairs, study the printed map. One learner asks, 'In which direction is the market from the school?' The partner answers in a full sentence.
2. Swap and give the direction to the health centre, the railway crossing and the footbridge.
3. With your teacher, open a digital map and search for a familiar place such as your school. Find the north marker before you describe a direction.
4. Write two sentences that use north, south, east or west.

## Practice
1. On most printed maps, which direction is at the top?
2. The railway crossing is south of the school. Write the direction you walk from the school to reach it.
3. Why should you check the compass rose on a digital map before you turn?
4. Write a sentence: The sun sets in the ____.

## Summary
• North, south, east and west tell us where places are.
• The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
• Use a digital map with an adult, and check which way is north.

### Answers to practice
1. North
2. Walk south.
3. The map may be rotated, so the top of the screen may not be north until you check the north marker.
4. The sun sets in the west.

questions.question: Which question helps you read a picture?
options: How many pages are in the book?
Who is in the picture and what is happening?
What is the writer's favourite colour?
questions.explanation: A visual is read by naming the people or objects and the action.

questions.question: In The Wet Road, why do the children use the footbridge?
options: To see the clouds more clearly
To stay off the wet road when a motorcycle is coming
questions.explanation: The comic shows them on the footbridge while a motorcycle uses the road.

questions.question: A path that goes under a busy road is called
questions.explanation: An underpass lets people pass underneath the road.

questions.question: At a railway crossing the barrier is down. What should you do?
options: Duck under the barrier and run
Wait until the way is clear
Stand on the tracks to see the train
Leave a bag on the tracks
questions.explanation: A lowered barrier means it is not safe to cross.

questions.question: A first aid poster shows a snake and an arrow to a hospital. The safe message is:
options: Cover the bite with a plaster and keep playing
Cut the bite and suck it
Keep the person still and get an adult to take them to hospital
Tie a tight band and wait at home
questions.explanation: A snake bite is an emergency. Do not cut, suck or tightly tie the limb.

questions.question: During a nosebleed the person should
options: lie down and tilt the head back
questions.explanation: Leaning forward helps keep blood from running down the throat.

questions.question: The sun rises in the
questions.explanation: Sunrise is in the east. Sunset is in the west.

questions.question: On the school map, the market is east of the school. The health centre is
questions.explanation: The map places the health centre to the north.

questions.question: Why do we learn to interpret visuals?
options: So pictures, maps and posters give us the right information
So we never need to read words
questions.explanation: A correct reading keeps the message clear and can keep us safe.

questions.question: Write one sentence giving a direction from the school to the footbridge on the map.
questions.answer: From the school, walk west to the footbridge.
questions.explanation: The footbridge is west of the school, so the direction sentence uses west.
